full_text.text: Background

The DRP1 protein, a member of the dynamin superfamily of GTPases, is encoded by the dynamin-1-like (DNM1L) gene and plays a critical role in mitochondrial fission. There was significant clinical heterogeneity in DNM1L-related disorders.
Methods

Whole exome sequencing (WES) was used to identify potential genetic causes of the phenotype in probands. Bioinformatics analysis was performed to analyze the pathogenicity of the identified variants, and 3D protein modeling was constructed to predict their effects on protein structure. Preliminary studies of the functional effects of the variant sites on the encoded proteins were performed by in vitro experiments.
Results

Two de novo variants, c.1049G>C (p.Gly350Ala) and c.2161C>T (p.Gln721*), were detected in affected individuals. One patient presented with severe epileptic encephalopathy while the other exhibited a distinctive clinical phenotype of hemiparesis. In silico analysis, conservative analysis, and 3D homology modelling indicated that the p.Gly350Ala and the p.Gln721* variants are deleterious. Furthermore, the results of the artificial transfection experiments demonstrated that the p.Gly350Ala variant resulted in a reduction in DNM1L expression at both the transcriptional and protein levels (p < 0.05). In contrast, the p.Gln721* variant exhibited no significant alteration in protein levels (p = 0.08), although it did result in a reduction in mRNA levels.
Conclusions

The present findings suggest that these variants may contribute to DRP1 deficiency, potentially triggering a range of DNM1L-related disease phenotypes. This study serves to expand the spectrum of variants associated with DNM1L-related disorders.
Introduction

Mitochondria undergo continuous fusion and division processes, which enable them to exhibit enhanced interaction behavior. The balance of fusion and fission is crucial for the maintenance of mitochondrial reticular morphology and the regulation of mitochondrial activity and function. Mitochondrial function is regulated by a dual genome comprising mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) along with nuclear DNA (nDNA). The mtDNA encodes a small fraction of the mitochondrial proteins, whereas the nDNA encodes more than 99% of the mitochondrial proteins that are synthesized in the cytoplasm and then transferred to the mitochondria. Clinical manifestations and genetic features of mitochondrial diseases are highly diverse. Mutations in genes associated with mitochondrial fission and fusion have been documented as a causative factor for certain neurodegenerative diseases. Furthermore, pathogenic variants that result in mitochondrial dysfunction have been linked to a spectrum of diseases, ranging from isolated optic atrophy to fatal encephalopathy.

DNM1L, located on the chromosome 12p11.21, is responsible for encoding GTPase dynamin-1-like protein (also referred to as dynamin-related protein 1 or DRP1), an important central effector in mitochondrial fission. DRP1 is a protein found in the cytoplasm. It moves to the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) and consists of a large GTPase domain, a middle domain, a non-conserved variable domain, as well as a GTPase effector domain (GED). These are involved in regulating GTPase activity and oligomerization. Upon activation, DRP1 is recruited to the OMM from the cytoplasm via receptors. Once at the OMM, DRP1 oligomerizes and hydrolyzes guanosine triphosphate (GTP), assembling into helical filaments which wrap and narrow the membrane. This process enables organelle division. Additionally, DRP1 mediates peroxisome fission, which is crucial for the maintenance of normal peroxisome morphology and function.

DRP1 impairment is linked to de novo dominant and compound heterozygous variants in DNM1L, which can lead to a severe neurological disorder known as encephalopathy due to defective mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission-1 (EMPF1, MIM#614388), in addition to isolated autosomal dominant optic atrophy 5 (MIM#610708). EMPF1 is characterized by early onset with developmental delay, progressive encephalopathy, dystonia (hypertonia or hypotonia), ataxia, and nystagmus. Furthermore, numerous patients present with refractory seizures and followed by a neurological decline and/or potentially fatal encephalopathy during childhood, indicating consistency with a lethal condition. On the whole, individuals with the DNM1L variant have a variable and unpredictable clinical course.

The phenotypic and genetic heterogeneity observed in mitochondrial diseases has led to molecular genetic testing becoming a crucial testing modality. However, novel sequence alterations may not be classified as either benign or pathogenic since there is a lack of functional evidence. In addition, there have been only 52 documented cases worldwide as of now, since Waterham et al. identified DNM1L in 2007. Further research is required in order to gain a more comprehensive understanding of this rare disease.

The present study describes a case series of two sporadic patients with de novo heterozygous variants (c.1049G>C, p.Gly350Ala and c.2161C>T, p.Gln721*) of the DNM1L gene. Although their clinical presentation is incompletely similar, we summarized their clinical features and follow-up information. Furthermore, bioinformatics analysis and in vitro functional experiments were employed to evaluate the effects of these two variants on the expression and stability of the DNM1L protein.
Materials and methods
Study subjects and ethical considerations

From 2020 to 2023, a total of two unrelated Chinese families were recruited to participate in this study. A comprehensive clinical data set was assembled, along with detailed family histories. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Children's Hospital Affiliated to Zhengzhou University (2024-K-081) and was conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Prior to the commencement of the study, written informed consent was obtained from both parents.
Whole-exome sequencing

As previously described, genomic DNA was extracted from the peripheral blood of the major members of both families. The processing and analysis of the WES data were conducted as described previously. Briefly, available DNA was sequenced on the Novaseq 6000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, USA) with 150 bp paired-end reads. The sequencing reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg19/GRCh37). The use of the Picard v1.57 software (http://picard.sourceforge.net/) enabled the removal of PCR duplicate sequences. The variant annotation and interpretation were conducted in accordance with the previously described methodology. Sanger sequencing was then performed to confirm potential disease-causing variants.
Bioinformatics analysis

To investigate the potential functional consequences of the different variants on the corresponding protein, pathogenicity prediction was conducted using REVEL (https://sites.google.com/site/revelgenomics/), FATHMM (http://fathmm.biocompute.org.uk/), and CADD (http://cadd.gs.washington.edu/score), respectively. All suspected variants were classified in accordance with the guidelines of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG). Amino acid sequences and 3D structure of the DNM1L1 protein (PDB: 5WP9, 4.22 A; PDB: 3W6O, 1.90 A) were obtained from the UniProt database (https://www.uniprot.org/) and Protein Data Bank (https://www.rcsb.org/). The MEGA11 software was utilized to analyse the degree of preservation, and the PyMOL software was employed to visualize the 3D structure of the protein.
Plasmid construction and transfection
The primers for plasmid construction, point mutation, and qRT-PCR

The entire sequence of DNM1L cDNA was cloned into the phage expression vector, which was purchased from Bioeagle Biotech Company. Wild-type (WT) cDNA plasmid (pcDNA3.1-Flag-EFla-copGFP-wt) was acquired by double digestion and ligation of the amplification products with pcDNA3.1-EFla-copGFP using a pair of amplification primers (DNM1L-BamHI-F/DNM1L-NotI-R). The WT plasmid was employed as a template for targeted mutagenesis using the Mut Express II Rapid Mutagenesis Kit V2 (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The sequences of primers used in these experiments are presented in Table 1. All the resulting recombination plasmids were verified via Sanger sequencing. For the transfection experiments, 293 T cells were incubated in six-well plates in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM; Gibco, Grand Island, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum at 37 C with 5% CO2. When the cells reached 70% - 80% confluence, the DNM1L-wt/mut plasmids (wild-type or mutated) were transfected into 293 T cell lines using Lipofectamine  3000 (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Following a 48-hour incubation period, total RNA and proteins were extracted from transfected 293 T cells for subsequent real-time quantitative PCR (qRT-PCR) and western blotting (WB) experiments.
Real-time quantitative PCR

Total RNA was extracted according to the manufacturer's protocol from Takara, Japan. DNM1L mRNA expression was then detected by qRT-PCR. The primer sequences are listed in Table 1. The relative mRNA expression levels of each dataset were processed by the 2-ddCT method and normalized to the housekeeping gene beta-Actin.
Western blot

The proteins derived from the transfected cells were collected and quantified utilizing a BSA reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, USA). Following standard operating procedures, polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis was performed. Then, the proteins were incubated with primary anti-DNM1L antibody (1:2000 dilution, Mabnus, Wuhan, China) and internal reference diluted with anti-GAPDH antibody (1:1000 dilution, Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, USA) at 4  C overnight. After washing, the blots were visualized with chemiluminescent substrate, followed by analysis via the Image J software.
Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses in this study were conducted using the Prism 8 software (GraphPad, La Jolla, USA). A t-test was employed to ascertain the statistical significance of the observed difference between the two groups, with p < 0.05 deemed to be the threshold for statistical significance.
Results
Clinical characteristics of patients
Clinical features of the probands

Patient 1 is the sole offspring of unrelated parents. She was born at full term following a pregnancy without incident and had a family history that presented no notable issues. The child was noted to have normal speech and motor development from the neonatal phase to three years of age. Nevertheless, her intellectual development was subpar in comparison to her peers (IQ = 62), and regular language developmental milestones were not achieved by the age of three (see Table 2). She was hospitalized at around 6.5 years old due to recurring nocturnal seizures caused by mountaineering. Following this, she exhibited persistent myoclonic status epilepticus in both lower limbs for two weeks, which improved with symptomatic treatment. Several tests were conducted to identify the cause of the epilepsy, but apart from a vitamin D deficiency, the other physical examinations and supporting tests were not indicative, including normal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and electroencephalogram (EEG). A seizure recurred about two months later, leading to admission to intensive care for refractory status epilepticus (RSE). Subsequently, she developed tremors, requiring assistance to walk even short distances, and experienced 1 to 2 seizures each day after waking from sleep.

When she was 6 years and 9 months old, a generalized tonic-clonic seizure (GTCS) associated with multifocal generalized epileptiform abnormalities were recorded through polymyographic video/EEG. Basal ganglia damage was shown in the brain MRI (data not shown), and laboratory tests suggested mildly elevated plasma lactate (2.58 mmol/L; reference range 0.7-2.1 mmol/L) as well as increased aspartate aminotransferase (49.05 U/L; reference range 13-35 U/L). However, hereditary aminoacidopathies and organic aciduria were ruled out. She had been administered coenzyme Q10 (100 mg/day), L-carnitine (1 g/day), vitamin B1 (300 mg/day), vitamin B2 (50 mg/day), vitamin C (600 mg/day), benzhexol hydrochloride (2 mg/day), and antiepileptic therapy. It is regrettable that, despite the absence of further deterioration in the patient's condition, the symptoms did not appear to improve with Coenzyme Q10 and L-carnitine treatment, as observed in the other patients mentioned in our previous article. At a recent assessment (7 years and 2 months), the child demonstrated comprehension skills and could recite stories, though her speech appeared to be slurred. Furthermore, motor regression with significant tremors was detected, and she was unable to sit on her own. Minimal sleep was observed; however, it seemed to be relatively more restful than previously reported.

Patient 2, a second child born to non-consanguineous Chinese parents, was delivered at full term with regular birth parameters. The detailed clinical features of the proband are as previously described. Briefly, she was delayed in speech development and developed left-sided limb dysfunction at the age of 1.5 years, which progressed to hemiparesis. Physical and ancillary examinations were unremarkable (see Table 2). Furthermore, a two-year follow-up study revealed that the administration of coenzyme Q10 (20 mg/d) and L-carnitine (1 g/d) was effective in addressing the patient's hemiplegic phenotype. Her current intelligence quotient (IQ) score is 75.
Identification of two novel variants in DNM1L
Variant identified in P.t 1 and prediction of pathogenicity of c.1049G>C

Family pedigrees and results of variants of the probands. The presence of the c.1049G>C (p.Gly350Ala) variant in P.t 1 and the c.2161C>T (p.Gln721*) variant in P.t 2 was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Both variants were de novo heterozygous. The arrow indicates the proband. Females and males are denoted by circles and squares, respectively

To identify potential pathogenic variants in patients, we performed parallel sequencing techniques. Sequencing of the mitochondrial DNA genome from blood-derived DNA of P.t 1 did not detect any possible pathogenic variants. Diagnostic analysis of the patient/parent trio using WES revealed a novel heterozygous c.1049G>C DNM1L (NM_012062.5) variant (see Fig. 1), resulting in the amino acid substitution NP_036192.2: p.Gly350Ala. The occurrence was confirmed as de novo through Sanger sequencing analysis. The de novo DNM1L c.1049G>C, p.Gly350Ala variant was classified as "Pathogenic" (see Table 3) according to ACMG criteria PS2, PM1, PM5, PS3_supporting, PM2_supporting, PP2, and PP3.

No pathologically significant variants were observed throughout the mtDNA genome of P.t 2. Trio-WES analysis of P.t 2 revealed an additional stop-gain variant, c.2161C>T, p.Gln721* in DNM1L (see Fig. 1). And the de novo DNM1L c.2161C>T, p.Gln721* nonsense variant was categorized as "VUS" according to the ACMG guidelines, using the criteria: PS2_Moderate, PM2_supporting, and PP3.

Location diagram and conservation analysis of DNM1L variants. A Schematic representation of DNM1L protein domains with localization of identified variants in patients (red font). B A comparison of the amino acid sequences of DNM1L proteins from different species. The amino acid sequences of the variant sites (c.1049G>C, p.Gly350Ala and c.2161C>T, p.Gln721*) are evolutionarily conserved and highlighted with a red box. C The 3D modeling of the protein of the DNM1L-wild and identified variants

Neither variant was identified in the 1000 Genomes Project, the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD), or the dbSNP database. The c.1049G>C (p.Gly350Ala) variant was predicted to be deleterious by online bioinformatics tools (see Table 3). A conservation analysis was conducted, which demonstrated that the positions of the c.1049G>C (p.Gly350Ala) and c.2161C>T (p.Gln721*) variants are highly conserved across different species (see Fig. 2B). Additionally, Fig. 2C presents the protein three-dimensional (3D) modeling of the DNM1L-wild and identified variants. As shown in Fig. 2C, the P.t 1 involves a G350 residue that adopts a phi angle of 89.7  and a psi angle of 19.6 , thus potentially disfavoring residues other than glycine. The substitution of glycine by a charged amino acid or other amino acids may result in unfavorable spatial conflicts with neighboring residues. Furthermore, the variant c.2161C>T (p.Gln721*) alters the spatial relationships of the DNM1L protein, resulting in the truncated protein losing its interaction with neighbouring amino acid residues, which may reduce the stability of the DNM1L protein.
Variants altered the transcript and protein levels of DNM1L

Functional consequences of the DNM1L variant in vitro. A and B Sequencing results showed that the c.1049G>C (p.Gly350Ala) and c.2161C>T (p.Gln721*) variants were successfully introduced; C The results of qRT-PCR revealed that the p.Gly350Ala and p.Gln721* variants caused a decreased mRNA transcript level compared to the WT (t-test, *:p < 0.05; **:p < 0.01); D and E The results of the WB analysis demonstrated that the p.Gly350Ala variant was associated with a reduction in protein levels, while there was no significant difference between the p.Gln721* variant and the WT (t-test, p = 0.08). All experimental results were based on three independent biological replicates

In order to investigate the functional impact of c.1049G>C (p.Gly350Ala) and c.2161C>T (p.Gln721*) variants, an artificial transfection system was constructed, followed by protein expression and qRT-PCR analysis. Sequencing in Fig. 3A and B confirmed the successful integration of the c.1049G>C (p.Gly350Ala) and c.2161C>T (p.Gln721*) variants. The results of qRT-PCR demonstrated a notable reduction in mRNA transcript levels for the p.Gly350Ala and p.Gln721* variants in comparison to the WT (p < 0.05, see Fig. 3C). Furthermore, as illustrated in Figs. 3D and E, WB assays demonstrated that the p.Gly350Ala variant resulted in decreased protein levels, in contrast to the p.Gln721* variant, which exhibited no significant difference compared to WT (p = 0.08).
Discussion

Since Waterham et al. reported in 2007 that DNM1L deficiency could cause mitochondrial disease characterized by global developmental delay and brain developmental abnormalities in infancy, significant progress has been made in comprehending DNM1L-related disorders. Subsequent studies have further revealed the phenotypic heterogeneity of DNM1L variants, with reported disease manifestations including early death, seizures, and dominant optic atrophy. Given the broad spectrum of disease outcomes observed in affected individuals, comprehensive characterization of novel disease-related genes and systematic pathogenicity studies are of critical academic and clinical significance. These efforts are essential for the precise interpretation and diagnosis of DNM1L variants, as well as for understanding how DNM1L variants alter physiology.

Pathogenic variants of DNM1L have been linked to a neurological disorder known as "EMPF1", with the core clinical features of developmental delay/regression, hypotonia, encephalopathy, seizures, ataxia, persistent lactic acidosis, and peripheral neuropathy. The present study investigated two patients with DNM1L variants, revealing phenotypic heterogeneity in disease severity. While both patients achieved normal developmental milestones in infancy, their subsequent clinical courses differed markedly. P.t 1 developed progressive severe epileptic encephalopathy, accompanied by global developmental delay, RSE, and basal ganglia damage. These symptoms are closely resembling those previously reported in DNM1L cases. In contrast, P.t 2 exhibited hemiparesis, a distinct clinical manifestation not previously described in DNM1L-associated disorders, thus expanding the phenotypic spectrum of DNM1L variants. Furthermore, treatment with coenzyme Q10 (20 mg/d) and L-carnitine (1 g/d) has been demonstrated to be efficacious in the management of the hemiplegic phenotype.

To date, over thirty pathogenic or likely pathogenic DNM1L variants have been reported, with more than 70% identified as de novo variants and over 60% localized to the middle domain. Clinical phenotype-genotype correlation studies have revealed domain-specific associations: variants in the middle domain are more frequently linked to severe manifestations such as RSE, as exemplified by Patient 1, who harbored a middle domain variant and presented with the RSE phenotype consistent with prior reports. In contrast, milder clinical phenotypes including optic atrophy and ataxia are linked to the GTPase domain. Consequently, the severity of the clinical phenotype might be related to the domain in which the DNM1L variants are located. Herein, we present our findings of two potentially pathogenic variants in the DNM1L gene, comprising a novel missense variant in the middle domain (p.Gly350Ala) and a novel stop-gain variant in the GED domain (p.Gln721*). These variants result in amino acid alterations at positions 350 and 721, respectively, which are highly conserved across the dynamin family and have not been documented in general population databases.

Pathogenic variants in the middle domain are typically associated with severe clinical and functional outcomes. For instance, the lethal variant in the middle domain of DRP1 (p.Ala395Asp) has been documented in neonates with microcephaly, lactic acidemia, and abnormal brain development. Mechanistically, missense variants in conserved amino acids, such as p.Ala395Asp and p.Gly350Asp, cause mitochondrial elongation in HeLa cells, resulting in impaired higher-order DRP1 protein assembly and function. Furthermore, Chao et al. identified a heterozygous variant (c.1048G>A) in the DNM1L gene leading to a p.Gly350Arg substitution at a greatly conserved residue within the middle domain. Functional analyses demonstrate that the introduction of the p.Gly350Arg variant in Drosophila lead to a dominant-negative effect, resulting in an increase in peroxisome size, an altered cellular distribution, and aberrant mitochondrial morphology and transport. Notably, P.t 1 in our study possessed a distinct missense substitution that impacted this amino acid (p.Gly350Ala). Although her clinical manifestations were consistent with the aforementioned case, follow-up records indicate she is currently alive. The different outcome between the two patients could be explained by different amino acid changes (p.Gly350Arg vs. p.Gly350Ala) or different inherited genetic backgrounds. Additionally, long-term monitoring of P.t 1 is essential to determine whether the p.Gly350Ala variant leads to other clinical outcomes.

Intramolecular interactions between the GEDs and the GTPase-middle domain, as well as the interactions between adjacent GEDs, are critical in regulating DRP1 GTP hydrolysis. Studies have demonstrated that pathogenic GED variants (p.Tyr691Cys, and p.Arg710Gly) could disrupt the GED-GTPase interactions, thereby impeding GED-GED assembly and reducing GTPase activity. Clinically, patients with GED variants generally display milder phenotypes compared to those with middle domain variants, such as seizures, impaired mobility, and optic atrophy. We have identified a de novo variant p.Gln721* in P.t 2, which is very close to the missense change reported previously. The patient did not exhibit the typical clinical manifestations observed in known GED variant cases; instead, a distinct phenotype was detected, which raises questions about the pathogenicity of p.Gln721*.

To further examine the functional effects resulting from these variants, we assessed the impact of DNM1L variants on mRNA and protein expression levels in vitro. The qRT-PCR analysis demonstrated that both variants cause a significant decrease in DNM1L expression at the transcriptional level compared to the WT (p < 0.05). Furthermore, the WB results revealed that the p.Gly350Ala variant resulted in decreased protein levels, whereas the p.Gln721* variant exhibited no significant difference in protein abundance relative to WT (Fig. 3D and E). Regarding the "nonlinear" relationship between mRNA and protein expression of the p.Gln721* variant, two hypotheses were proposed to explain this phenomenon: (1) As a very late truncation variant, p.Gln721* is expected to escape nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), leading to the production of stable truncated proteins; (2) DNM1L proteins have been demonstrated to induce dominant negative gain-of-function in DNM1L-related mitochondrial diseases, where sufficient protein levels exert an effect on complex function. While mRNA levels are decreased (~ 30%), this reduction is insufficient to lower protein abundance below a functional threshold. Consequently, we speculate that the variant's pathogenicity likely stems from the dominant negative effect of truncated DNM1L proteins (e.g., impaired GTPase activity and oligomerization with wild-type monomers), rather than mRNA reduction itself. However, the results of functional experiments also cast doubt on the pathogenicity of the p.Gln721* variant. For instance, under the assumption that p.Gln721* is a loss-of-function (LOF) variant, this heterozygous mutation would result in a 50% reduction in protein expression. However, this finding is inconsistent with the experimental results obtained. Consequently, we hypothesise that this variant may not meet the PVS1 criteria, which would consequently necessitate its reclassification as a VUS.

Nevertheless, it should be noted that this study is not without its limitations. Firstly, the absence of residual material from patients renders the applicability of the artificial transfection system we have created to human disease states uncertain. Therefore, the effects of the p.Gly350Ala and p.Gln721* variants on mitochondrial and peroxisomal morphology in patient cells and/or artificially transfected cells warrant further investigation. Secondly, Chang et al. reported that mutations at position 350 of DNM1L disrupt DRP1 oligomerization and the formation of fission complexes, potentially leading to DRP1 degradation in isolated mitochondria. Importantly, however, total cellular protein expression levels of the mutant DRP1 did not differ significantly from those of the wild-type [30]. In contrast, the present study observed a reduced expression of the p.Gly350Ala variant at the total cellular protein level, a phenomenon distinct from the above-described scenario. This discrepancy is speculated to result from decreased mRNA stability, such as degradation caused by structural abnormalities, although this hypothesis awaits further experimental validation.

In conclusion, two de novo DNM1L variants were identified in this study. The results of in silico analyses and functional experiments suggest that the variants may contribute to some extent to DRP1 defects, which may trigger the emergence of a range of DNM1L-related disease phenotypes. Encouragingly, P.t 2 appears to exhibit the mildest clinical phenotype to date, and long-term follow-up will be conducted to understand the progression and outcome of DNM1L-related disorders. Furthermore, considering the clinical heterogeneity of mitochondrial disorders, more clinical data and functional studies of DNM1L variants are needed to elucidate the genotype-phenotype correlations of DNM1L-related disorders. It is also recommended that DNM1L variants be considered in cases of developmental delay, epilepsy, dystonia, and/or hemiparesis.
Neurodevelopmental Phenotype Associated with TRIP12: Report of a Family Carrying the p.Asp1135Val Variant

Background: Pathogenic variants in the TRIP12 gene are associated with Clark-Baraitser syndrome, a condition characterized by neurodevelopmental disorders, including intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and speech delay. Phenotypic expression is variable, and facial features are not consistently present. Familial inheritance is rare. Methods: Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed on a proband with speech disorder and ASD, as well as on her parents. Clinical assessment included developmental, cognitive, and physical evaluations. Results: A heterozygous missense variant c.3404A>T (p. Asp1135Val) in the TRIP12 gene was identified in both the proband and her father. Both presented with speech disorder and ASD without facial features or severe intellectual disability. Conclusions: In line with recent genotype-phenotype studies, missense TRIP12 variants tend to be associated with milder neurodevelopmental presentations, typically characterized by mild to moderate intellectual impairment, variable autistic traits, limited or absent facial features, and a low incidence of epilepsy. This familial case further presents the phenotypic spectrum of TRIP12 missense variants and highlights that ASD and speech disorder may occur as isolated neurodevelopmental findings without syndromic features. The report reinforces the relevance of TRIP12 analysis in the differential diagnosis of ASD and language disorders, even in individuals lacking physical traits, supporting more accurate genetic counseling and broader awareness of inherited TRIP12-related conditions.
1. Introduction

The TRIP12 gene (Thyroid hormone receptor-interacting protein 12, OMIM 604506), located on chromosome 2q36.3, encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase belonging to the HECT (Homologous to E6-AP C-Terminus) family. This enzyme plays a key role in the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway, which is fundamental for maintaining protein homeostasis and regulating essential processes such as cell cycle progression, DNA damage response, chromatin remodeling, and cell differentiation. Pathogenic variants in the TRIP12 gene disrupt E3 ligase activity, with downstream effects on neurodevelopmental processes. These variants were first linked to Clark-Baraitser syndrome (OMIM #617752), initially described in 1987 in a mother and two sons with intellectual disability (ID), obesity, and facial features.

Subsequent studies have shown that de novo or inherited TRIP12 variants cause variable intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), epilepsy, and sometimes dysmorphic traits. Intellectual disability is reported in 100% of individuals with pathogenic TRIP12 variants, with cognitive performance ranging from mild to severe. Among individuals carrying pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in the TRIP12 gene, around half present with autistic features, supporting the classification of TRIP12 as a high-confidence autism spectrum disorder (ASD) gene in resources such as SFARI (Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative), which ranks genes based on the strength of evidence linking them to ASD. A hallmark feature of the TRIP12-associated neurodevelopmental phenotype is speech and language impairment, often coexisting with apraxia of speech (CAS). In one cohort of 17 probands with pathogenic TRIP12 variants, 88% had expressive language difficulties, ranging from single words to a complete absence of verbal language. The clinical phenotype associated with TRIP12 shows marked variability. While some patients present with recognizable facial features reminiscent of Clark-Baraitser syndrome, others show no obvious physical features. Inherited variants are associated with milder phenotypes; pathogenic variants inherited from an affected parent (often with mild intellectual disability) may present with more severe manifestations in offspring. At the molecular level, TRIP12 contains a catalytic HECT domain essential for ubiquitin ligase activity, as well as WWE and ARM domains that mediate protein-protein interactions. Missense variants affecting critical regions (e.g., within the HECT domain) may reduce protein stability or alter enzymatic activity, often correlating with more severe phenotypes, including regression and lower cognitive and language outcomes. This report describes a familial case of the c.3404A>T; p.Asp1135Val (NM_004238.3; rs778262518) TRIP12 variant in a father and daughter, both presenting with speech impairment and a diagnosis of ASD (DSM-5 severity level 1), but without dysmorphic features. This case further broadens the understanding of the TRIP12-associated clinical spectrum, highlighting the phenotypic variability, absence of classic facial features in some familial cases, and the significance of inherited variants.
2. Case Presentation

The proband (21-year-old female) presented with a history of speech disorder and features consistent with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), without facial features or severe intellectual disability. Psychological assessment revealed difficulties in reciprocal social interaction, restricted interests, and avoidance behaviors. Personality evaluation confirmed introversion, social discomfort, and emotional withdrawal. Her father (51-year-old male) exhibited a similar neurobehavioral profile, with lifelong speech difficulties, social avoidance, and milder ASD traits (Figure 1). The diagnosis of ASD in both the proband (ADOS-2 score = 11) and her father (ADOS-2 score = 9) was established according to DSM-5 criteria, integrating clinical observation with standardized neuropsychological assessment tools. Neither presented with congenital malformations, abnormal growth patterns, or distinct facial dysmorphism. However, anthropometric data and photographs could not be included as the family did not authorize publication of identifiable clinical information; nonetheless, specialist evaluation confirmed the absence of notable physical or facial anomalies. The family history revealed two paternal relatives who developed dementia at an advanced age, although no genetic testing was performed on these individuals (Figure 1). Both the proband and her father underwent genetic testing to investigate possible underlying causes of their condition, and the proband's mother was also tested to assess variant segregation within the family. Trio-based whole-exome sequencing (WES) was performed, along with chromosomal microarray analysis (array-CGH), on DNA extracted from peripheral blood of all three individuals. WES, covering approximately 19,000 genes, identified a heterozygous TRIP12 c.3404A>T (p.Asp1135Val; rs778262518) variant in both the proband and her father, while the mother tested negative, supporting paternal inheritance (Figure 1).

Only variants of uncertain significance (VUS) with a pathogenicity score >= 3.5 were considered for further evaluation. This threshold, based on eVai's integrated ACMG/AMP criteria scoring system, is associated with an expected sensitivity > 96% and specificity > 99%, and reflects a higher likelihood of reclassification toward pathogenicity pending additional clinical or functional evidence. Array-CGH excluded pathogenic copy number variations (CNVs). No other variants meeting ACMG/AMP criteria for pathogenicity, likely pathogenicity, or high-scoring variants of uncertain significance (VUS) related to the investigated Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms including HP:0001249 (Intellectual disability), HP:0000717 (Autism), HP:0001263 (Global developmental delay), HP:0000750 (Delayed speech and language development), HP:0011098 (Speech apraxia), and HP:0002546 (Incomprehensible speech) were detected.

FMR1 testing for Fragile X syndrome was also negative. In the context of p.Asp1135Val variant interpretation, TRIP12 demonstrates strong evidence of intolerance to both missense and loss-of-function variation. As of August 2025, no records in ClinVar and no prior peer-reviewed case reports describe this exact variant associated with phenotype; it is present only in population datasets (ExAC/EVA 2015; gnomAD/TopMed/ALFA updates through 2024) at very low allele frequency (gnomAD v2.1.1: 7/244,660; AF = 2.86 x 10-5; 0 homozygotes). According to gnomAD constraint metrics, the missense z-score of 6.366 indicates marked depletion of this missense variant. The pLI score of 1 (LOEUF = 0.145) confirms high intolerance to loss-of-function. These constraint metrics, combined with segregation of the variant in two affected family members, align with a likely pathogenic classification according to ACMG and AMP criteria, pending functional confirmation. Structural assessment shows that p.Asp1135Val is located in exon 2 within a well-structured region of the TRIP12 protein, with a per-residue pLDDT confidence score above 90 in the AlphaFold model, indicating high reliability of the predicted local conformation. This residue is situated outside both the WWE domain (residues 759-847) and the HECT catalytic domain (residues 1712-1992). Pathogenicity prediction tools further support the relevance of this variant: AlphaMissense assigns a score of 0.967 to p.Asp1135Val, consistent with a high predicted pathogenic potential. The variant results in the replacement of a negatively charged aspartic acid residue with a hydrophobic valine residue within a structured region of the protein. This substitution can disrupt local electrostatic interactions or hydrogen bonding networks and may alter protein stability or conformational dynamics. AlphaMissense is a computational model that integrates sequence conservation, structural environment of the residue, and physicochemical changes introduced by the mutation to estimate the probability of pathogenicity. Evolutionary conservation of the Asp1135 residue was evaluated through phylogeny-based metrics integrated in the annotation pipeline, including PhyloP, PhastCons and GERP++, all of which indicate that this position is highly conserved across vertebrate species. However, clinical correlation and functional assays will be required to clarify its impact on E3 ligase activity and neurodevelopmental phenotypes. In summary, whole-exome sequencing detected approximately 36,000 variants per individual; among these, the heterozygous p.Asp1135Val variant in the TRIP12 gene was the only one that met the clinical relevance criteria in both the father and the daughter.
3. Discussion

Missense TRIP12 variants, particularly those located in the HECT catalytic domain, have been recurrently associated with disruption of E3 ligase activity, impairing ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation and leading to neurodevelopmental consequences.

Based on variants reported in the HGMD, ClinVar and DECIPHER databases as of November 2025, the majority of pathogenic TRIP12 alterations are loss-of-function (LoF), while missense variants represent a smaller proportion of the overall mutational spectrum. Pathogenic missense changes tend to cluster within functionally constrained regions, most notably the WWE and HECT domains, highlighting their relevance to TRIP12 protein function. Across all variant classes, the most recurrent clinical features include intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, developmental delay and marked speech impairment, consistent with the core neurodevelopmental phenotype associated with TRIP12 dysfunction.

Functional hypotheses suggest that such alterations can reduce protein stability, disrupt substrate interactions, or alter enzymatic turnover, ultimately affecting neuronal maturation, synaptic homeostasis, and transcriptional regulation. Nobakht et al. (2025) further propose that reduced protein stability may trigger a compensatory upregulation of TRIP12 mRNA levels, partially mitigating the biochemical impact and explaining milder phenotypic presentations in some cases.

Familial TRIP12 variants often manifest as milder, non-syndromic phenotypes compared to de novo variants. Aerden et al. (2023), in the largest cohort described to date, confirmed that inherited missense variants tend to present with less severe intellectual impairment, absence of epilepsy, and frequent lack of craniofacial dysmorphism, although subtle facial features may occasionally be observed. This variability is reflected in our family, where both affected individuals presented with ASD and speech disorder without facial features. The current case parallels previous reports by Bramswig et al. (2017) and Donoghue et al. (2020), in which language delay and ASD were cardinal findings across different TRIP12 genotypes, with physical features absent or mild in some inherited cases. Our identification of the p.Asp1135Val variant in two affected relatives, both showing similar but relatively mild neurodevelopmental manifestations, supports the view that certain TRIP12 variants can result in an attenuated, familial form of the disorder.

Zhang et al. (2017) originally described TRIP12 haploinsufficiency as a cause of intellectual disability and ASD, highlighting variable expressivity even within the same family. This variability likely reflects a combination of consequences (missense versus truncating variants, domain affected), compensatory mechanisms (e.g., mRNA upregulation), and possible modifying genetic or environmental factors.

Given the extensive genetic heterogeneity that characterizes neurodevelopmental disorders, including global developmental delay, intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder, and the considerable clinical overlap among these conditions, the diagnosis of TRIP12-related syndrome cannot rely on single-gene tests. Even when suggestive clinical features are present, exome sequencing or an exome-based neurodevelopmental panel represents the most appropriate diagnostic approach, as it allows the identification of TRIP12 variants within a highly complex genetic landscape.

Our case also emphasizes the importance of constraint metrics in variant interpretation: the high missense z-score (6.366), pLI = 1 (LOEUF 0.145), and extremely low pRec (5.6379 x 10-38) and pNull (1.397 x 10-64) provide strong evidence of intolerance to missense and LoF variation, further supporting pathogenicity under ACMG/AMP criteria. To our knowledge, this report represents the first description of TRIP12 c.3404A>T (p.Asp1135Val; rs778262518) associated with a neurodevelopmental phenotype.

Overall, this case expands the phenotypic spectrum of TRIP12-associated disorders by reinforcing that missense variants can present in a familial form with ASD and speech disorder, without physical features. Such findings are crucial for genetic counseling, as they underline the need to consider TRIP12 analysis even in patients without the classic Clark-Baraitser facial features, particularly when there is familial recurrence of ASD or language impairment.
4. Conclusions

This is, to the best of our knowledge, the first report linking TRIP12 c.3404A>T (p.Asp1135Val; rs778262518) to a neurodevelopmental phenotype (ASD and speech disorder). These findings warrant deposition and public sharing of this variant with phenotypic details to facilitate future case aggregation and curation. This familial case of the TRIP12 p.Asp1135Val (rs778262518) missense variant expands the clinical spectrum of TRIP12-associated neurodevelopmental disorders. Both affected individuals presented with speech disorder and ASD without facial features, consistent with the milder phenotype often observed in inherited missense variants. The absence of facial features underscores the phenotypic variability of TRIP12 variants and supports the inclusion of TRIP12 in the genetic evaluation of ASD and language disorders. Recognition of such cases is important for genetic counseling, as familial TRIP12 variants may confer a risk for recurrence of mild neurodevelopmental phenotypes without syndromic presentation. Continued aggregation of familial cases and functional characterization of variants will be essential to clarify genotype-phenotype correlations and refine prognostic counseling.

LEO1 haploinsufficiency is associated with developmental delays and autism spectrum disorder
full_text.title: Subject terms

full_text.text: LEO1 encodes a core subunit of the evolutionarily conserved RNA polymerase associated factor 1 complex (PAF1C), a key regulator of eukaryotic gene expression. While burden analyses suggest an association between rare LEO1 variants and an increased risk for neurodevelopmental disorder, the paucity of reported cases has prevented a definitive characterization of the resulting phenotype. We describe a male child with a novel de novo frameshift variant in LEO1 c.446dup (p.Asp149Gluf s*2) and undertake a comprehensive phenotype delineation of all previously reported patients. Developmental delay and autism spectrum disorder were core features common across patients with truncating variants, though rarer manifestations were also observed. This analysis supports LEO1 haploinsufficiency as a mechanism for this neurodevelopmental disorder. Further research is needed to more completely ascertain its associated features and penetrance. We nevertheless encourage its recognition as a definitive disease gene and inclusion in multigene panels.

LEO1 encodes a core subunit of the evolutionarily conserved RNA polymerase associated factor 1 complex (PAF1C), a key regulator of eukaryotic gene expression. PAF1C physically associates with RNA polymerase II and is integral to the transcription cycle, including elongation, mRNA 3' end formation, processing, and chromatin modification. The complex also orchestrates RNA polymerase II degradation in response to DNA damage. Despite their operating as a complex, each PAF1C subunit has functional specialization, with LEO1 regulating heterochromatin stability and histone H3 turnover during cellular quiescence. In addition, LEO1 is critical during embryogenesis in model organisms, where homozygous knockout of leo1 in zebrafish leads to severe defects in cardiac and neural crest development and in mice is associated with preweaning lethality.

Burden analyses in cohorts of neurodevelopmental disorder patients have identified significant enrichment for rare variants in LEO1. This association is supported by the substantial fraction of neurodevelopmental disorders in humans occurring in genes within transcription and chromatin remodeling pathways, including other PAF1C subunits. Nevertheless, the reported LEO1 variants to date have included a combination of truncating variants expected to result in a loss-of-function, missense variants, and paternally inherited promoter deletions that paradoxically appear to cause gene overexpression. In addition to the paucity of reported cases, the limited clinical data available for each proband has prevented a more definitive characterization of the resulting phenotype.

Here, we report the case of a male child with a de novo frameshift variant in LEO1, providing further evidence that haploinsufficiency of this gene is associated with an increased risk for neurodevelopmental impairment. This is reinforced by the comprehensive phenotype delineation we undertake of all previously reported patients.

The proband is the first liveborn child to a nonconsanguineous couple of Cuban and Japanese descent. He was born at 30 weeks gestation following a pregnancy complicated by intrauterine growth restriction, with a weight of 1.0 kg (z = -1.24), length of 38 cm (z = -0.48), and head circumference of 28 cm (z = 0.32). During his admission to the NICU he developed respiratory distress and apnea of prematurity, which was managed with oxygen supplementation. Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed normal biventricular size and systolic function. He was discharged home at 2 months of age. At 18 months old he was still not using any words. The brain MRI performed at that time was interpreted as normal. He also had persistent spit-ups with feeding, though evaluation with a swallow study and esophagram found no impairment, indicating a functional disorder. He was ultimately diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, as he exhibited oral aversion to foods, deficits in social communication, and fine motor impairments, for which he received feeding, speech, and occupational therapies, respectively. By age 5 he was able to feed himself independently, speak in complete sentences, read multi-syllabic words, count to ten, identify colors, and trace letters. His medical history was otherwise only significant for reactive airway disease and recurrent respiratory infections requiring multiple hospitalizations. Physical examination did not reveal craniofacial dysmorphisms or physical anomalies. Neither his parents nor his seven half-siblings are similarly affected.

His genetic workup included chromosomal microarray and Fragile X testing, which was unrevealing. Trio exome sequencing of the proband and his unaffected parents was performed at an accredited commercial laboratory, GeneDx (Gaithersburg, MD). This identified that he is heterozygous for a single base pair duplication in exon 2 of LEO1 (NM_138792.4:c.446dup) (NP_620147.1:p.Asp149Gluf s*2). No other variants were reported. Our analysis found the LEO1 variant is absent in the Genome Aggregation Database (gnomAD v4.1.0) (PM2). Neither of his confirmed parents harbored the variant, establishing that it occurred de novo in our proband (PS2). As such, we determined that our proband's LEO1 variant meets criteria for a likely pathogenic classification using the ACMG guidelines for the interpretation of variants.
Comparison of our proband's phenotype with all previously reported affected individuals heterozygous for a LEO1 truncating variant as well as non-truncating variant

We next compared the clinical history of our proband to the six previously reported patients with LEO1 truncating variants (Table 1). Analysis of the variant position within the gene suggested that each would lead to nonsense-mediated decay of the mRNA (Supplementary Fig. 1). Three of these previously reported truncating variants were also confirmed to have occurred de novo, providing additional evidence of their pathogenicity. A consistent phenotype in our proband and the previously described patients was observed, with neurodevelopmental impairments that included developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder, and intellectual disability in the absence of structural brain anomalies. Congenital hypotonia as well as ADHD were also described in a minority of cases, and one patient had a history of microcephaly, seizures and an abnormal gait. Additional manifestations described in only single cases included extraocular muscle dysfunction, disordered sleep, cryptorchidism, and proximal muscle weakness.

Finally, our analysis was expanded to include the nine previously reported patients with missense and splice site variants, as well as promoter deletions (Table 1). In three of these cases, the LEO1 variant was inherited from an unaffected parent, with the remainder occurring de novo. These patients had a broader range of clinical findings that included craniosynostosis and craniofacial dysmorphisms, as well as cardiac anomalies and hearing loss, albeit in a minority of cases. Their most frequent manifestations, however, also included developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder, and intellectual disability, overlapping with the truncating variant patients.

Based on this detailed clinical characterization of a proband and independently ascertained cases with de novo loss-of-function variants, we conclude that LEO1 haploinsufficiency is responsible for a neurodevelopmental disorder. This is further supported by the gene's intolerance to loss-of-function variants in gnomAD v4.1.0 (pLI = 0.99, LOEUF = 0.49). In addition, we provide the initial delineation of the LEO1-related phenotypic spectrum, which includes core features common across variant types, as well as less common manifestations that may be variant-specific or, conversely, unrelated to the disorder. Larger cohorts of affected patients will need to be described to better define the broader neurodevelopmental risks of the LEO1-related syndrome and its associated penetrance, as the lack of clinical data in previous reports represents a significant limitation to current estimates. Functional studies should work towards describing how LEO1 haploinsufficiency leads to transcriptional dysregulation and more clearly demonstrate the molecular consequences of non-truncating variants, including promoter deletions. Nevertheless, we recommend that LEO1 be recognized as a disease gene with strong evidence of causation and be included in multigene panels for developmental delay and autism spectrum disorder.
RNA Analysis Uncovers Pathogenic PARN Variant in Dyskeratosis Congenita
ABSTRACT

Dyskeratosis congenita (DC) is a rare genetic disorder caused by impaired telomere maintenance, leading to diverse clinical manifestations, including bone marrow failure, mucocutaneous abnormalities, and multi-organ dysfunction. Here, we report a 14-year-old male patient presenting with microcephaly, developmental delay, synostoses, cerebellar hypoplasia with ataxia, and an immunodeficiency condition, but lacking classical DC features such as nail dystrophy and skin hyperpigmentation. WGS revealed two variants in the PARN gene: a known pathogenic missense variant (c.1045C > T, p.Arg349Trp) and a novel intronic variant (c.178-28T > C). Functional RNA analysis demonstrated that the intronic variant disrupts the branch point sequence, leading to exon 4 skipping and nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of a significant proportion of transcripts. This study confirms the pathogenicity of the intronic variant and underscores the importance of functional validation in interpreting noncoding variants, particularly in genetically heterogeneous disorders like DC. Our findings expand the molecular and phenotypic spectrum of PARN-related DC and highlight the utility of WGS reanalysis and RNA studies in resolving diagnostically challenging cases.

Using WGS and RNA analysis, we identified a branch point-disrupting variant in the PARN gene and elucidated its pathogenic molecular mechanism in a child with atypical dyskeratosis congenita presentation.
Introduction

Dyskeratosis congenita (DC) is a rare, progressive disorder inherited in an autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, or X-linked pattern. The primary clinical features of DC include reticulate hyperpigmentation, nail dystrophy, and oral leukoplakia. Additional variable somatic abnormalities may also occur, including pulmonary, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, cerebral, and dental complications. DC can be diagnosed when a patient presents with at least two of the four primary clinical features (nail dystrophy, abnormal skin pigmentation, leukoplakia, and bone marrow failure) along with at least two additional extra-hematopoietic features. Determining the specific type of DC based solely on clinical symptoms or laboratory findings is challenging due to the clinical heterogeneity of the disorder and the varying degrees of symptom severity.

DC belongs to a group of diseases known as "telomere biology disorders," which are caused by germline mutations in genes regulating telomere maintenance. To date, pathogenic variants in 18 different genes have been identified as causes of DC.

One of the genes that regulates telomerase stability is PARN. Biallelic variants in PARN are associated with a DC autosomal recessive 6 (OMIM#616353) and Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome, the most extreme manifestation of DC.

In this study, we describe a patient with microcephaly, accompanied by delayed psychomotor and speech development, synostoses, cerebellar hypoplasia with ataxia, and an immunodeficiency condition. Through WGS, we identified two variants in the PARN gene: a previously reported pathogenic missense variant and a novel intronic variant. Using RNA analysis, we demonstrated the pathogenicity of the intronic variant in the PARN gene and identified its mechanism of action.
Materials and Methods
This section is shown in Supporting Information.
Results
Clinical Findings

A boy was born to non-consanguineous parents with no significant family history. He was born at 39 weeks of gestation. Delivery was normal (Table 1). From 3 months, there were complaints of poor weight. Early motor development was delayed. At 2 years of age, microcephaly was diagnosed. From the age of 3 years, frequent respiratory diseases of severe course, recurrent stomatitis, and purulent rhinosinusitis were observed. Immunological tests revealed signs of combined immunodeficiency with T-regulatory disorders since 5 years of age (Figure 1A,B). At 8 years of age, the possibility of Nijmegen syndrome was suggested. Analysis of common pathogenic variants in the NBN gene was normal.
Anthropometric parameters and laboratory data (from birth to 12 years).
(A) The spectrum of clinical manifestations in the proband and their age of onset. (B) Patient's appearance.

At 9 years of age, the patient was hospitalized: blood tests showed no signs of cholestasis and cytolysis; hepatic protein synthesis function was preserved. There were no signs of autoimmune processes. Elastography results detected hepatic fibrosis F0-F1. MRI and MRCPG showed no significant liver enlargement and moderate affecting of liver parenchyma, with enhanced vascular pattern. Gastroscopy revealed pangastritis, jejunum inflammation, and lymphofollicular hyperplasia of the terminal part of the sigmoid colon. Blood tests revealed thrombocytopenia. The bone age of the 9-year-old patient was delayed and was approximately 7-7.5 years. Ultrasound examination showed signs of hepatomegaly with diffuse parenchymal changes and dysfunction of the bile ducts.

At 12 of age the patient was examined: blood tests revealed a slight elevation in transaminases, with no signs of compromised protein-synthetic liver function or coagulopathy. Moreover, bone marrow aspirate analysis showed signs of myeloid hypoplasia, erythroid hypoplasia, dyserythropoiesis, and granulocytic hypoplasia. MRI of the sacroiliac joints showed multiple areas of signal intensity changes detected in the lateral masses of the sacrum and in the bodies of the iliac bones on both sides. These areas appear hyperintense on STIR imaging, indicating fatty conversion of the bone marrow. Brain MRI revealed hypoplasia of the corpus callosum. Colonoscopy detected lymphofollicular hyperplasia of the terminal ileum mucosa. Liver electrography detected fibrosis F1 (METAVIR). Oral leukoplakia was misdiagnosed as aphthous stomatitis. Flow cytometry revealed the patient's telomere length was reduced to 2.7% (reference range: 8.2%-16.2%).
Molecular Findings

Whole-genome sequencing was performed in a trio format on the proband and his parents. However, no pathogenic variants meeting the search criteria were identified. The WGS data were reanalyzed 2 years later. Two variants in the PARN gene were revealed: a previously reported pathogenic variant in exon 16 of the PARN gene, NM_002582.4(PARN):c.1045C > T, leading to a missense substitution (p.Arg349Trp) and a novel variant NM_002582.4(PARN):c.178-28T > C in intron 3 (Figure 2B).

(A) Pedigree of the reported family. (B) Sanger sequencing confirmed the WGS-identified variants. (C) The sashimi plot illustrates the results of deep targeted RNA sequencing (proband, mother, control). The proband showed significantly increased PARN exon 4 skipping versus mother and control. (D) The c.1045C > T variant in the proband's genomic DNA sequencing (top panel) and targeted RNA sequencing (bottom panel). The RNA sequencing data demonstrates allelic imbalance of the c.1045C > T variant (59%/41%).

The c.1045C > T variant has previously been reported as pathogenic. The authors of the study demonstrated that this substitution reduces the protein's deadenylation activity, consequently impairing its function. The variant c.178-28T > C is classified as a VUS based on its absence in the gnomAD (v.4.1.0) population database. Sanger sequencing validated the WGS results, confirming the variants occur in trans: c.1045C > T (maternal) and c.178-28T > C (paternal) (Figure 2B,C).

Homozygous and compound-heterozygous pathogenic variants in the PARN gene have been reported in patients with DC type 6. Given that many of the symptoms characteristic of this disease matched the clinical presentation of the proband, we decided to analyze the pathogenicity of the intronic variant.

We performed a comprehensive computational analysis of the c.178-28T > C variant using SpliceAI, SpliceAPP, ESEfinder, and HExoSplice. SpliceAI analysis yielded a potential weakening of both donor and acceptor splice sites flanking exon 4, potentially causing exon 4 skipping. HExoSplice and ESEfinder failed to detect any significant regulatory elements within the variant-containing locus. SpliceAPP analysis, integrating both bioinformatic predictions and experimental evidence, identified the variant's location within the branch point region of PARN intron 3. To verify this prediction, we performed RNA analysis of the PARN gene using RNA isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells from the proband and his mother. The father's blood samples were unavailable for RNA analysis. RNA from the PBMCs of a healthy individual was used as a control.

Sashimi plot analysis revealed that the proband expressed both the canonical PARN transcript and an aberrant isoform with complete exon 4 skipping, accounting for 28% of total transcripts (Figure 2D). At the protein level, this splicing defect results in a premature termination codon (p.His60ValfsTer7), truncating 574 C-terminal amino acids. It is noteworthy that a similar isoform was found in the proband's mother, who does not carry the c.178-28T > C variant, and in the control sample. Investigation of GTEx Portal transcriptomic data reveals that this alternatively spliced transcript exhibits constitutively low expression in hematopoietic tissue. However, the level of transcripts with exon 4 skipping did not exceed 3%.

Targeted RNA-analysis of locus with c.1045C > T variant revealed that the variant was in a state of allelic imbalance (WT/mut = 41/59) in the proband; whereas no allelic imbalance was detected in his mother (Figure 2C). This data suggests a reduction in the expression of the allele containing the c.178-28T > C variant, which may result from transcript degradation via the NMD (nonsense-mediated decay) mechanism.
Based on the cumulative data, this variant was characterized as likely pathogenic according to ACMG criteria (PM2, PS3, PM3) and the underlying cause of the patient's clinical presentation.
Discussion

In this study, we described a patient with a nonspecific set of clinical features that did not allow for a definitive clinical diagnosis or targeted genetic testing. At 3 months of age, the patient exhibited poor weight gain; by 1 year, delayed physical development was noted; and by 2 years, microcephaly was diagnosed. Starting at age 3, frequent respiratory infections and recurrent stomatitis suggested:and later confirmed:immunodeficiency with T-regulatory disorders.

For patients with such nonspecific clinical presentations, WGS is the diagnostic method of choice. However, even with this approach, only 40% of patients receive a definitive molecular diagnosis, which is attributed to the incomplete understanding of gene structures, functions, and their association with pathological phenotypes.
Moreover, despite the broad spectrum of clinical manifestations characteristic of DC, many symptoms may manifest years later; this significantly complicates clinical diagnosis.

In our case, the family has been repeatedly evaluated by a geneticist; the following conditions have been excluded: chromosomal abnormalities, hereditary aminoacidurias, mitochondrial diseases, hereditary epilepsies, Miller-Dieker syndrome, Joubert syndrome, Cockayne syndrome, Nijmegen breakage syndrome, Nicolaides-Baraitser syndrome, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and cystic fibrosis.

The initial trio WGS analysis failed to identify pathogenic variants accounting for the proband's clinical presentation. At the first evaluation, the proband lacked overt manifestations of primary immunodeficiency (PID), with microcephaly representing the predominant clinical feature. Thrombocytopenia had been interpreted as secondary to liver fibrosis with associated portal hypertension and splenomegaly. However, subsequent comprehensive investigations excluded portal hypertension, demonstrating that thrombocytopenia instead reflected intrinsic hematologic abnormalities rather than hepatic pathology. The absence of pathogenic findings in the initial analysis likely resulted from the exclusive focus on genetic causes of isolated microcephaly. Importantly, microcephaly co-occurs with PID in numerous syndromic conditions, and immunodeficiency may remain clinically silent for prolonged periods before manifesting overt symptoms. Based on these observations, it can be concluded that systematic immunological evaluation is necessary for all patients presenting with microcephaly prior to initiating molecular genetic testing.

Based on additional clinical data, reanalysis of the proband's WGS data identified two variants in the PARN gene: one pathogenic variant c.1045C > T and one variant of uncertain clinical significance c.178-28T > C.

To date, only a few dozen patients with DC type 6 (associated with pathogenic PARN variants) have been described, leaving the full clinical spectrum and genotype-phenotype correlations poorly understood. Moreover, among the most characteristic features reported in the literature:such as abnormal skin hyperpigmentation and nail dystrophy :none were present in our proband. Meanwhile, microcephaly, observed in our proband, is neither a common nor a mandatory criterion for DC type 6. The incomplete overlap with previously reported cases, combined with the uncertain significance of one variant, made a definitive diagnosis challenging.

Through bioinformatic and RNA analyses, we demonstrated that the c.178-28T > C variant leads to exon 4 skipping in the PARN gene due to disruption of the branchpoint site and triggers NMD-mediated degradation of a subset of transcripts. These findings allowed the reclassification of c.178-28T > C as pathogenic. Thus, the patient was found to carry two pathogenic PARN variants, enabling a conclusive molecular diagnosis.

It is worth noting that the detection and interpretation of noncoding variants pose particular challenges. According to the literature, only three intronic variants outside canonical splice sites have been reported in PARN to date: c.1319-16T > A, c.659+4_659+7delAGTA, and c.98-6A > G. Notably, none have undergone functional validation.

Our findings demonstrate the critical role of WGS reanalysis coupled with functional studies in resolving atypical presentations, particularly for genes with poorly defined genotype-phenotype correlations.
Clinical and Genetic Analysis of SMARCC2-Related Diseases in Three Chinese Patients
ABSTRACT
Background

Coffin-Siris syndrome (CSS) is a rare, clinically and genetically heterogeneous disorder characterized by coarse facial features, microcephaly, intellectual disability (ID), developmental delay (DD), and hypo/aplastic digital nails and phalanges, typically of the 5th digit. CSS is an autosomal dominant disease resulting from mutations in genes encoding components of BRG1/BRM-associated factor (BAF) chromatin remodeling complexes. More than 300 CSS patients have been reported with variants in genes in the BAF pathway. Recently, patients carrying SMARCC2 variants have been reported to be associated with CSS8. However, as the number of cases increases, many patients do not exhibit the representative clinical symptoms of CSS. Additional case reports and clinical studies will contribute to a redefinition of SMARCC2-related disorders.
Methods

In this research, three patients with SMARCC2-related disorders from China were recruited. Genomic DNA was extracted from the peripheral blood leukocytes of these patients' parents and other family members, and then subjected to whole-exome sequencing as well as Sanger sequencing.
Results

In the present study, two de novo variants (c.1311-3C>G, c.347G>A (p.Arg116His)) and a novel de novo variant (c.346C>T (p.Arg116Cys)) in the SMARCC2 gene were detected in three patients with neurodevelopmental disorders by whole exome sequencing. The clinical presentation of our patients supports a redefinition of SMARCC2-related diseases, which include mild to moderate DD, mild ID, facial dysmorphism, mild speech delay, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, brain abnormalities, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and autistic behaviors. Furthermore, both the type of variant and its specific location may be contributing factors influencing the clinical outcomes.
Conclusion

Our study expands the genetic spectrum of SMARCC2 variants and detailed genotypic and phenotypic descriptions are important for the diagnosis of SMARCC2-related disease and accurate clinical management.

In this article, we investigate the pathogenesis of three unrelated Chinese children who exhibited mild to moderate developmental delay, mild intellectual disability, facial dysmorphism, mild speech delay, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, brain abnormalities, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and autistic behaviors. Furthermore, both the type of variant and its specific location may be contributing factors influencing the clinical outcomes. Our study expands the genetic spectrum of SMARCC2 variants, and detailed genotypic and phenotypic descriptions are important for the diagnosis of SMARCC2-related disease and accurate clinical management.
Introduction

Coffin-Siris syndrome (CSS) is a rare group of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD) with an estimated incidence of 1:10,000-1:100,000. It is characterized by a range of developmental delay (DD), intellectual disability (ID), growth retardation, microcephaly, speech impairment, coarse facial features, hypertrichosis, sparse scalp hair, hypoplastic nails of the fifth finger and/or toe, and brain anomalies, the most prominent of which is hypoplasia or agenesis of the corpus callosum (Kosho et al. ; Coffin and Siris ). According to available reports, the clinical and genetic manifestations of individuals with CSS are heterogeneous, with most cases being sporadic and showing autosomal dominant inheritance (Kosho et al. ). CSS is caused by variants in genes encoding components of the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling BRG1-associated factor (BAF) complex (the mammalian SWI/SNF complex). Within this family of genes, de novo pathogenic variants in ARID1A, ARID1B, ARID2, DPF2, SMARCC2, SMARCA4, SMARCE1, and SMARCB1 have been identified in patients with CSS (Santen, Aten, et al. ; Tsurusaki et al. ; Vasileiou et al. ; Wieczorek et al. ; Van Houdt et al. ; Bramswig et al. ; Machol et al. ). In addition, de novo variants in the SOX11 and SOX4 genes were observed in individuals with clinical phenotypes consistent with CSS (Tsurusaki et al. ; Zawerton et al. ). Several of these genes are also associated with other ID/NDD (Santen, Kriek, and van Attikum ). Thus, additional reports on variants in these genes will help us better understand the phenotype spectrum and the relationship between genotype and phenotype.

Recently, heterozygous variants in the SWI/SNF-related, matrix-associated, actin-dependent regulator of chromatin subfamily c member 2 (SMARCC2) gene were described as underlying Coffin-Siris syndrome 8 (CCS-8; MIM: 618362), characterized by ID and multiple malformations (Machol et al. ). The SMARCC2 gene, located at 12q13.3, encodes a core subunit of the chromatin remodeling complex BAF, BAF170. The protein SMARCC2 consists of MarR-like (10-136), BRCT (140-183), SWIRM (424-521 aa) and SANT domains (596-647 aa) and plays an essential role in embryogenesis and cardiac development (Hota et al. ). To date, more than 60 individuals with SMARCC2 gene variants have been identified (Figure 1A, Table S1; Machol et al. ; Li et al. ; Yi et al. ; Carss et al. ; Sun et al. ; Chen et al. ; Lo et al. ; Gofin et al. ; Bosch et al. ). The phenotypes of these patients are heterogeneous, including mild to severe ID, growth retardation, prominent speech delay, behavioral abnormalities, hypotonia, feeding difficulties, skin problems, brain abnormalities, and dysmorphic features, including hypertrichosis, thick eyebrows, thin upper and thick lower vermillion, and upturned/anteverted nostrils. These features overlap with those observed in other NDD, such as CSS and Nicolaides-Baraitser syndrome. Thus, additional reports on these gene variants will help us better understand the spectrum of the resulting phenotypes and the genotype-phenotype relationship. Herein, we report two de novo variants (c.1311-3C>G, c.347G>A (p.Arg116His)) and a novel de novo variant (c.346C>T (p.Arg116Cys)) in the SMARCC2 gene (NM_003075.3) in three Chinese patients with NDD (Figure 1B), and further provide a detailed description of the associated clinical features of these patients.
